To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
adequacy of family resources is related to both well being and commitment to early intervention treatments.

adequacy of family resources is positively related to maternal well-being and commitment of mothers to professionally prescribed child level interventions even after the effect of maternal age, child age and developmental status, family socioeconomic status, and family income are statistically removed.

mothers of developmentally-delayed infants and toddlers who have more family resources report higher well-being and are more committed to the early intervention program than mothers with fewer resources.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the hypothesis that adequacy or adequacy of resources, personal well- being, and adherence to professionally-prescribed child- level regimens are related.
the hypothesis that family resources are related to personal well being and adherence to professionally-prescribed child-level regimens.
the question of how the family's resources are related to the family's commitment to the early intervention program and its child-level regimens.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the adequacy of family resources is a significant predictor of maternal well-being and commitment.
the more resources a family has, the more likely the family will be able to provide the child with an environment that will enhance the child's development.

the adequacy of resources available to a mother in the form of social support and financial support is related to both her well-being and her ability to adhere to professionally prescribed treatments for her child.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
families with adequate resources have higher levels of personal well-being and commitment.
the adequacy of a family's resources is related to the well-being of the family members and to the family's commitment to the child's treatment regimen.
families with adequate resources are more committed to child-level treatments and have greater well-being.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we need to help families identify their own needs and help them meet those needs before asking them, or expecting them, to carry out professionally-prescribed child level interventions as part of their participation in early intervention programs.
families are the experts on their own needs.
the more resources you have, the more likely you are to have a higher quality of life and the better able you will be to adhere to the recommendations of your healthcare providers.
